name: Cloudflare
summary: A global reverse-proxy network that puts a CDN, DNS, DDoS protection and a WAF in front of your site.
intro: Cloudflare works by taking over your domain’s DNS. You point the domain’s nameservers at Cloudflare and mark records as “proxied”. A lookup then returns one of Cloudflare’s anycast IP addresses instead of your server’s, so every visitor connects to the nearest Cloudflare data center (Cloudflare lists more than 340 cities). That data center terminates TLS, filters attacks, answers from cache if it can, and only then forwards the request to your origin, whose real IP stays hidden.

The difference from a classic CDN is that caching is one feature on a general proxy. The same hop runs the WAF, bot filtering, rate limiting, load balancing and Workers scripts, and every plan, including the free one, gets unmetered DDoS mitigation with no bandwidth bill. By default it caches by file extension (images, CSS, JS, fonts and so on) but not HTML or JSON; you opt those in with cache rules. Tiered Cache lets edge locations ask an upper-tier data center before your origin, and a cache lock collapses simultaneous misses into one origin request.
strengths: Free plan includes the CDN, DNS and unmetered DDoS mitigation, with no charge for bandwidth
Security and caching live on one hop, configured in one place
Hides your origin’s IP address, so attackers can’t bypass the proxy as easily
Pairs with Workers and R2 to run code and store files on the same network
limits: Doesn’t cache HTML or JSON until you add cache rules, which surprises people who expect full-page caching
Terms let Cloudflare limit sites that serve video or mostly large files through the CDN without paid products like Stream, Images or the Developer Platform
Outside Enterprise, the largest cacheable file is 512 MB and the origin read timeout is fixed at 125 seconds
Proxied records have a fixed 300-second TTL, and the normal setup makes Cloudflare your DNS provider

story: Cloudflare grew out of a side project about spam. In 2004 Matthew Prince and Lee Holloway built Project Honey Pot, which let any website owner track how spammers harvested email addresses. Thousands of sites joined, and their most common request was: don’t just track the bad guys, stop them. In 2009, at Harvard Business School, Prince met Michelle Zatlyn, who saw a business in doing exactly that. The name came from the idea of a “firewall in the cloud”.

The founders wanted to give everyone, from individual developers to large companies, the speed, protection and reliability that “only the likes of Google, Amazon, and Facebook could afford”. Their trick was to sit in front of a website as a proxy: change your domain’s nameservers and traffic flows through Cloudflare, no code or hardware needed. They launched at TechCrunch Disrupt on 27 September 2010 with five data centers, and hundreds of sites signed up before the judges finished their questions.

From that proxy Cloudflare kept adding services on the same hop: free TLS for every customer in 2014, the Workers edge runtime in 2017, the 1.1.1.1 public resolver in 2018. It went public on the NYSE in September 2019.

choices.why: Taking over DNS let Cloudflare route a site’s visitors through its proxy without the owner installing anything, which made a self-serve, free product possible.
Every data center announces the same addresses, so visitors reach the nearest one and an attacking botnet’s traffic is split across all of them instead of hitting one site.
A huge base of free sites gives Cloudflare early sight of new attacks, an instant test bed for new features, and the traffic that makes ISPs want to peer with it at no cost.
Since 2017 DDoS mitigation has been unmetered on every plan. Cloudflare argued that charging victims more during an attack was wrong, and its network had grown big enough to absorb the largest ones.

timeline.text: Prince and Holloway start Project Honey Pot to track spammers
Cloudflare founded; wins the Harvard Business School business plan competition
Public launch at TechCrunch Disrupt on 27 September

Unmetered DDoS mitigation on all plans; Workers announced
IPO on the New York Stock Exchange as NET
Announces plans to become a public certificate authority with post-quantum certificates
